questions.stem: A prescription reads methotrexate 2.5 mg daily for rheumatoid arthritis. What is the best action?

options.text: Call the prescriber: it should be weekly for arthritis

questions.explanation: C is correct: for non-cancer uses like arthritis, oral methotrexate is weekly; daily dosing by mistake has caused deaths. A and B dispense a daily regimen. D makes the dosing even more frequent.

questions.stem: Which practices help prevent oral methotrexate errors? Select all that apply.

options.text: Name the day of the week
Dispense daily for arthritis if the patient insists
Reserve daily oral dosing for specific cancer regimens

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and E are correct: default to weekly, name the day, teach back, and keep daily oral methotrexate for specific cancer regimens. D is wrong because daily dosing for arthritis is a dangerous error, no matter who asks.

questions.stem: Why should units be written out in insulin orders instead of the letter U?

options.text: The letter U can look like a zero

questions.explanation: A is correct: the letter U can look like a zero, turning 10 units into 100. B, C, and D are not the reason for the rule.

questions.stem: How should concentrated insulin, 500 units per mL, be given?

options.text: With its own dedicated syringe or pen

questions.explanation: D is correct: concentrated insulin needs its own dedicated syringe or pen. A risks a fivefold dosing error. C and B are not how this insulin is given.

questions.stem: An order reads: concentrated potassium chloride by IV push. What is the best action?

options.text: Never give it by IV push; it must be diluted
Give it into the muscle instead

questions.explanation: C is correct: concentrated potassium chloride is never pushed into a vein; it must be diluted. A is still an IV push. B follows a dangerous order. D is not how potassium chloride is given.

questions.stem: A fentanyl patch is prescribed for a patient who has never taken opioids. What is the best action?

options.text: Call the prescriber because the patient is not opioid tolerant

questions.explanation: C is correct: fentanyl patches are only for opioid-tolerant patients. A dispenses an unsafe start. B is wrong because a patch must never be cut. D adds naloxone but still starts an unsafe drug.

questions.stem: A patient asks if they can cut a fentanyl patch to use a smaller dose. What is the best answer?
questions.explanation: C is correct: never cut a patch. A, B, and D all cut the patch.

questions.stem: Which patients on opioids should be prescribed or offered naloxone? Select all that apply.

options.text: A patient on high opioid doses
A patient taking an opioid with a benzodiazepine
A patient using topical lidocaine only

questions.explanation: A and B are correct: naloxone is offered to patients at higher risk of overdose, such as high doses or use with benzodiazepines. C, D, and E are not taking opioids.

questions.stem: Why are names printed as hydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE?

options.text: Tall-man lettering shows the difference between look-alike names
The capital letters show the dose
They show the drug is high-alert

questions.explanation: A is correct: tall-man lettering uses capital letters to show the difference between look-alike names. B, C, and D are not what the capital letters mean.

questions.stem: A drug usually taken once weekly arrives with directions for daily use. What is the best action?
questions.explanation: B is correct: when a weekly drug shows up as daily, stop and call. A dispenses a possible overdose. C changes the order without the prescriber. D does not fix the directions.
